chapters.title: Chapter 3: Correlation, Diversification, and the Multi-Asset Risk Engine

lessons.title: Covariance, Not Just Correlation: Why Volatility-Adjusted Relationships Matter

body.text: Correlation tells you the shape of how two assets move together. It says nothing about how big those moves actually are. Two asset pairs can share the exact same correlation and still contribute wildly different amounts of actual risk to a portfolio, because risk depends on magnitude as much as it depends on direction, and that is exactly what covariance captures and correlation alone does not.

children.text: This chapter has built the correlation matrix as its central tool, and for reading which assets move together and which decouple, correlation is the right tool. But Chapter 6's risk parity strategy, and portfolio construction generally, cannot be built on correlation alone. This closing lesson of Chapter 3 shows exactly why, converts Lesson 4's correlation matrix into a full covariance matrix, and uses it to demonstrate one of this course's most important practical results: equal capital weighting does not produce equal risk.
Correlation Is Scale-Free; Portfolio Risk Isn't

Correlation is deliberately normalized to sit between -1 and 1, which makes it easy to compare across any pair of assets regardless of how volatile each one individually is. That normalization is also exactly what strips out the information a risk model actually needs. A correlation of 0.3 between two assets each moving 5% a year describes a very different amount of actual co-movement, in real terms, than a correlation of 0.3 between two assets each moving 25% a year. Portfolio risk is measured in real units, rupees or percentage points of value at stake, not in the unitless -1 to 1 scale correlation lives on.
From Correlation Matrix to Covariance Matrix

Converting a correlation matrix into a covariance matrix just means putting the volatility back in: multiply each correlation by the volatilities of the two assets involved. Applying this to Lesson 4's illustrative correlation matrix, using annualized volatilities of 20% for Nifty, 12% for Gold, 6% for G-Sec futures, and 7% for USD-INR, produces the covariance matrix below, in percent-squared units.

body.caption: Covariance matrix from correlation matrix. D is a diagonal matrix of volatilities (20, 12, 6, 7 here), rho is the correlation matrix from Lesson 4. Each entry Sigma_ij equals rho_ij times sigma_i times sigma_j.

body.text: This covariance matrix is derived arithmetically from Lesson 4's illustrative correlation matrix and the illustrative volatility figures given here, not from actual computed historical data. The mechanics shown apply identically once you plug in real numbers.

children.text: Why This Matters: Risk Contribution Isn't Proportional to Weight

markDefs.definition: The share of a portfolio's total variance attributable to a specific asset, calculated as the asset's weight multiplied by the covariance-weighted sum of its relationship with every asset in the portfolio, divided by total portfolio variance. Risk contributions across all assets sum to 100% of total variance.

children.text: Take an equal-weight portfolio, 25% each in Nifty, Gold, G-Sec futures, and USD-INR, and compute each asset's

using the covariance matrix above. The portfolio's total variance works out to about 38.9%², giving a portfolio volatility of roughly 6.2%. Breaking that total variance down by asset produces a result equal capital weighting completely conceals.

body.caption: Equal-Weight (25% Each) Portfolio: Capital Weight vs Risk Contribution

body.label: Equal-Weight 4-Asset Portfolio Volatility
body.context: Derived from the covariance matrix above; despite equal 25% capital weights, Nifty alone drives nearly 60% of this portfolio's total risk

body.text: Equal capital weight is not equal risk. In this illustration, a quarter of the portfolio's capital sits in Nifty, but well over half of its risk does, simply because Nifty is both the most volatile instrument in the book and only modestly correlated with the others. Chapter 6 builds risk parity specifically to correct this, sizing positions so that risk contribution, not capital, ends up balanced across the book.

children.text: What This Sets Up for Chapter 4 Onward

This closes Chapter 3's risk engine: measuring correlation properly, understanding how different crisis types break it differently, building a valid correlation matrix, and now converting that into the covariance matrix that actual portfolio construction runs on. Chapter 4 shifts from measuring risk to generating return signals, starting with trend-following across each asset class individually. The covariance and risk-contribution machinery built here does not disappear once signals enter the picture, it is exactly what Chapter 6 uses to turn a set of individual signals into one properly sized multi-asset portfolio.

body.title: The Desk That Thought It Had Balanced Risk
body.scenario: A newly formed systematic desk allocates capital equally across four instruments: 25% Nifty 50 futures, 25% Gold, 25% G-Sec futures, and 25% USD-INR, describing this allocation as "balanced" to their investment committee. A committee member, familiar with this chapter's material, asks them to actually compute each position's contribution to total portfolio risk before presenting the allocation as balanced.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson's illustrative numbers, was the desk's "balanced" description accurate? What should they present to the committee instead?
body.modelAnswer: No, the description was not accurate in the sense that matters for risk. Equal capital weight, 25% in each instrument, produced a portfolio where Nifty alone contributed roughly 58.5% of total variance, while USD-INR, despite the identical 25% capital weight, contributed only about 2.4%. The book is capital-balanced but risk-concentrated, dominated by its most volatile, least-hedged-against-the-rest instrument. What the desk should present instead is the risk contribution breakdown itself, capital weight alongside risk contribution for each asset, since that is the number that actually describes how exposed the portfolio is to any single instrument's bad day, and it is the number Chapter 6's risk parity approach uses to correct exactly this kind of mismatch.

body.title: Verifying Gold's Risk Contribution
body.prompt: In this lesson's equal-weight example, Gold's contribution to total variance is w_Gold × (Σw)_Gold = 0.25 × 48.45 = 12.11 (in %²). Given total portfolio variance of approximately 38.93 (%²), what percentage of total portfolio risk does Gold contribute? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 12.11 / 38.93 ≈ 0.311, or 31.1%. Gold holds the same 25% capital weight as every other asset in the book, but contributes nearly a third of total portfolio risk, well above its capital share, because of its meaningful volatility and its modest positive correlation with Nifty and G-Secs in this matrix.

body.title: Correlation vs Covariance
body.question: What is the key piece of information covariance captures that correlation, on its own, does not?
options: Whether two assets move in the same or opposite directions
The magnitude of co-movement, since covariance incorporates each asset's actual volatility, not just the normalized -1 to 1 direction and strength of the relationship
Correlation and covariance are mathematically identical measures
Whether an asset class is traded in India or internationally
body.explanation: Correlation is normalized to a unitless -1 to 1 scale, which is useful for comparing relationships across very differently sized assets but strips out how large the actual co-movement is in real terms. Covariance restores that by multiplying correlation back through by each asset's volatility, which is exactly why portfolio risk calculations, and Chapter 6's risk parity sizing, run on covariance rather than correlation alone.

points: Correlation is normalized and scale-free; it describes the shape of co-movement but not its magnitude, which is exactly what a risk calculation needs
Covariance restores that magnitude: Sigma_ij equals rho_ij times sigma_i times sigma_j, or in matrix form, Sigma equals D rho D
Equal capital weighting does not produce equal risk; in this lesson's illustrative 4-asset book, Nifty's 25% capital weight drove nearly 60% of total portfolio risk
Risk contribution, an asset's share of total portfolio variance, is the number that actually describes portfolio balance, not capital weight alone
This gap between capital weight and risk contribution is precisely the problem Chapter 6's risk parity approach is built to solve

Chapter 3 closes here having built the full risk engine, correlation measurement, crisis-type awareness, the correlation matrix, and now the covariance matrix, that every strategy from Chapter 4 onward is sized against
